A.explanation: At balance $E$ equals the p.d. across $0.64\text{ m}$ of the wire, which is $0.50\text{ V}$ after allowing for the driver internal resistance.

B.explanation: This is the p.d. across the whole $0.96\text{ m}$ wire XY, not across the $0.64\text{ m}$ balance length XZ.

C.explanation: This ignores the $0.50\,\Omega$ internal resistance and uses $1.5\text{ V}$ across the wire, giving $(0.64/0.96) \times 1.5 = 1.0\text{ V}$.

D.explanation: This is too large and cannot be balanced by only part of the wire when the full wire p.d. is less than $1.5\text{ V}$.

hints: Notice the driver loop contains two resistances in series: the $0.50\,\Omega$ internal resistance and the $0.50\,\Omega$ wire XY.
First find the driver current from $1.5\text{ V}$ and the total $1.0\,\Omega$ resistance, then find the p.d. across the full wire XY.
At zero galvanometer reading, $E$ equals the p.d. across length XZ only, so scale the XY voltage by $0.64\text{ m} / 0.96\text{ m}$.
walkthrough: Identify the driver circuit: $1.5\text{ V}$ cell drives current $I$ through its $0.50\,\Omega$ internal resistance plus the $0.50\,\Omega$ uniform wire XY.
Calculate $I$ with $I = E / R_{total}$: $R_{total} = 0.50 + 0.50 = 1.0\,\Omega$, so $I = 1.5 / 1.0 = 1.5\text{ A}$.
Find the p.d. across the whole wire XY: $V_{XY} = I \times R_{XY} = 1.5 \times 0.50 = 0.75\text{ V}$.
Use uniformity of the wire: p.d. is proportional to length, so $V_{XZ} = V_{XY} \times XZ/XY = 0.75 \times 0.64/0.96$.
At balance no current flows in the test cell branch, so $E = V_{XZ} = 0.50\text{ V}$. This is option A.
